title: About 45 `async def` UI routes run their SQLite writes on the event loop; one click during a collector write freezes every request on the dashboard for up to 5 s
where: `dashboard/src/ccsync_dashboard/account_ui.py:481-702` (display-name, session revoke, revoke-others, machine settings ask/withdraw); `ui.py` async routes at 1270, 1493, 1556, 2368, 2621, 2662, 2709, 2890, 3002, 3186, 3235, 3252, 3275, 3282, 3420, 3537, 3631, 3684, 3725, 3764, 3810, 3840, 3858, 3888, 3912, 3938, 3991, 4010, 4070, 4667, 4713, 4750, 4795, 4838, 4868, 4894 (list from `grep -A2 "^async def" | grep get_conn`)
what: these routes are `async def` only so they can `await request.form()`, but they take a `get_conn` connection (default `busy_ms=5000`) and run their reads, writes and commit inline, on the one event loop of the `--workers 1` container. A write that meets a held write lock sleeps inside sqlite's busy handler with the loop thread blocked. This is the CR-282F / bug-dash-auth-2 shape through a third door: both of those fixed one call site each (the 500 handler, the session touch), the routes were never swept.
cost: an admin presses any of these (tick for someone, push an update, resume lane B, approve a key, rename themselves) while the collector or a companion report holds the write lock. Every other request in the process - every companion `/api/v1/report`, every htmx poll on every tab, every Cards fetch - waits until the lock clears or 5 s pass, and then the click itself 503s. Frequency is bounded by admin clicks x the fraction of time a write lock is held (CR-351 measured multi-second writes before its fix; still 0.1-1 s per big report after it).
evidence: `probe_loop.py`: with another connection holding `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for 3 s, the display-name POST took 3.08 s and a `GET /partials/halt-line` scheduled 0.2 s after it was not even SENT until 3.07 s (the loop could not wake its own `asyncio.sleep`), answered at 3.08 s. Without the held lock both take ~5 ms.
ledger: new (same mechanism as CR-282F and bug-dash-auth-2, both FIXED for their own call sites only)
fix: keep the `await request.form()` in the async handler and move everything after it into one `await run_in_threadpool(work, ...)` (the pattern `partial_account_password` and `partial_admin_display_name`'s users view already use), or parse the form in an async dependency and make the route a plain `def`. A test that holds the write lock and asserts a concurrent GET answers in < 0.5 s pins the class. Must not change the CSRF gate's reliance on body_size_gate having buffered the body (form parsing stays where it is).

title: The home page and its polls rebuild the whole projects view 12 times a minute per open tab, and the page itself builds every view twice
where: `ui.py:925-966` (`page_fleet`), `templates/fleet.html:27-28` (`home_readouts`, `home_tree` template globals), `ui_home.py:170-181` (`_plan_facts_for` opens its own connection and rebuilds the transfers view), `ui_home.py:296-368` (`home_tree` opens its own connection and calls `build_projects_view` again: `projects_view` is never passed), `ui.py:2811-2817` (`/partials/fleet` builds the projects view for the overview + OOB readouts every 15 s), `ui_home.py:436-453` (home-queue, every 10 s), `ui_home.py:406-413` (projects-tree, every 30 s); the per-build cost sits in `api.py:464-497` (`build_projects_view`: `db.fetch_projects` is one device/completion query PER PROJECT, and `_editor_view` -> `_lanes_view` recomputes the same (editor, machine) lane chips for every (project, editor) row)
what: `page_fleet` builds `build_projects_view` once and shares it with `_sidebar_context` and the queue (the DASH-6 fix), but the terminal template then calls `home_tree`, which opens a fresh connection and builds the projects view a second time, and `home_readouts`, which opens another and builds the transfers view a second time. `_sidebar_context`'s output is itself recomputed by `tree_context`. On the polls, three of the home windows each rebuild the projects view independently, and inside each build the lanes for an (editor, machine) are re-derived once per project that editor ticked.
cost: measured on this desktop (the NAS CPU is slower). `GET /` as admin: 2 projects-view builds, 2 transfers-view builds, 7 connections, 1,170 SQL statements, 39 ms at 100 projects / 89 ms at 500. Per visible admin home tab per minute: fleet 4 x (25-38 ms) + queue 6 x (15-30 ms) + tree 2 x (14-36 ms) = 12 projects-view builds; with the 2 s transfers poll, the tab costs ~700 s of server CPU per day at 100 projects and ~1,150 s/day at 500 (0.8-1.3 % of a core, per tab, 24 h on a wall display), all of it GIL-serialised with the report handlers. `fetch_projects` is 100 statements per build at 100 projects (500 at 500). In the profile, `_lanes_view` is 8,600 calls per 10 page renders and ~57 % of `build_projects_view`'s time (lane_chip + `age_seconds` ISO parsing). The backlog half of `build_transfers_view` is PRAC-73 (open) and not counted again here; my seed had no `editor_media`, so these numbers are the floor.
evidence: `probe_prof.py` "builder calls per request: build_projects_view 2, build_transfers_view 2, build_editors_view 1"; `probe_sql.py`: `/partials/fleet` 602 statements (100 of them the per-project device query), `/partials/home-queue` 178 (100), `/partials/projects-tree` 121 (100); `probe_builders.py` timings above.
ledger: related to DASH-6 (bug-hunt-2026-08-14; its second half, "collapse db.fetch_projects' N+1", was never done) and PRAC-73 (open, the transfers/backlog half)
fix: (a) pass the handler's `projects_view` and `transfers` into the template and have `home_tree` / `home_readouts` take them (one build each per page, ~40 % of the page); (b) in `build_projects_view`, compute `_lanes_view` once per (editor, machine) and reuse it per row (estimated -50 % per build); (c) one `completion_current JOIN devices` query grouped in Python instead of the per-project query; (d) optionally memoise the projects view per request-scope for ~2 s, since three windows of one tab ask for it within the same 30 s. All four keep the "one snapshot per render" property DASH-6 established.

title: The service worker revalidates content-hashed, immutable assets on every navigation and rewrites them into CacheStorage each time
what: every `/static/` request under the worker is answered from cache AND re-fetched with `{cache: 'no-cache'}`, including `?h=<hash>` URLs whose bytes cannot change. Per the Fetch spec a revalidated 304 comes back to the worker as the stored 200, so `res.ok` is true and `cache.put` rewrites every asset on every navigation. The `immutable` header that `CachedStaticFiles` sets is therefore dead for every secure-context client (anyone on Tailscale Serve https, i.e. every phone and the installed PWA). And because `activate` only deletes caches with another NAME, a same-version redeploy that changes hashes leaves the old `?h=` entries in the cache until the next VERSION bump.
cost: a dashboard page loads about 19 static URLs (shell: 4 sheets, 6 scripts, 2 favicons, apple-touch icon; page: 2; 4 fonts from the sheets). Each navigation therefore costs ~19 conditional requests (each ~1.9 ms server time through the middleware stack, measured, plus a tailnet RTT each) and ~0.5 MB of CacheStorage writes on the phone, for nothing. An editor clicking through 50 pages a day: ~950 wasted requests and ~25 MB of flash writes per device per day.
evidence: code path read; `probe_home.py` shows the hashed URL is served `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` and that a conditional request answers 304.
ledger: new (the SWR rule is dash-mounts-ui-5 / dash-mounts-ui-b-3; this keeps it for un-hashed URLs)
fix: in the `/static/` branch, if the URL carries `h=`, return a cache hit with no revalidation (cache-first; fetch and put only on a miss), and when putting a hashed URL delete cached entries for the same pathname with a different `h`. Keep stale-while-revalidate exactly as it is for un-hashed URLs (the PRECACHE list, fonts), which is the case dash-mounts-ui-5 exists for.

title: Five `@app.middleware("http")` (BaseHTTPMiddleware) layers: +0.9 ms on every request and half the throughput on every streamed byte
what: each `@app.middleware("http")` is a Starlette `BaseHTTPMiddleware`, which runs the inner app in a task group and pipes the response body through an anyio memory stream. Five are stacked, so every request pays five task spawns and every response chunk crosses five streams. The mounted apps' own gates were already written as plain ASGI for this reason (`broll.py:204`, `music.py:158`, `ytdl.py:144`); the parent's own five were not.
cost: a static asset through the full app took 1,937 us vs 1,069 us through a bare mount of the same `CachedStaticFiles` (+0.87 ms, +81 %). A 200 MB `FileResponse` streamed at 294 MB/s through 5 no-op layers vs 693 MB/s with none: every media byte the dashboard serves in-process (b-roll previews, music audio, Cards audio/video, `/api/v1/companion/package/` downloads of 40-120 MB, the sorter's thumbnails) costs ~2.4x the event-loop CPU. At a tailnet's ~50 MB/s that is ~17 % of a core per active stream instead of ~7 %.
evidence: `probe_mw.py`, `probe_stream.py`.
fix: fold the five into ONE `@app.middleware("http")` function that runs the same checks in the same order (outermost first: login gate, expiry stamp, body-size gate, stale-page gate, CSRF), or rewrite them as one plain ASGI class. Must keep: body_size_gate buffering and re-arming the body before csrf_gate reads the form, and login_gate resolving the session before the expiry stamp. Short-circuit `/static/` at the top so assets skip everything.

title: Each authenticated request opens a fresh SQLite connection on the event loop just to look up the session; connection setup is 25-75 % of a poll's server time
where: `auth.py:755-802` (`_resolve_session` -> `sessions.validate_ex`), `sessions.py:262-345` (`_run` opens `db.connect` per call), `db.py:710-728` (`connect` issues 4 PRAGMAs every time, including `journal_mode=WAL`, which is persistent in the file); `ui.py:783`, `806`, `819`, `ui_home.py:174`, `358`, `375` (each opens its own connection in the same request)
what: `login_gate` is async, so the session SELECT (connect + 4 PRAGMAs + query + close) runs on the loop for every non-static request; then the route's `get_conn` opens a second connection in the threadpool; `_render` and the template globals open more. `GET /` as admin opens 7.
cost: connect + 4 PRAGMAs + SELECT + close = 1,524 us; the same SELECT on a held connection = 4 us. `/partials/halt-line` (polled every 60 s on every page) takes 4.0 ms of which ~3 ms is the two connection setups; `/partials/stamp` the same every 30 s. Across one admin home tab (~67,700 requests/day, all signed in) that is ~100 s/day of event-loop time spent opening connections for the session check alone, more on ZFS where opening the -wal/-shm files is slower (estimated).
evidence: `probe_mw.py`; `probe_home.py` connection counts (`/` admin connects=7, every partial >= 2).
ledger: new (sessions.py's own comment records why the touch got a short busy timeout; this is the read beside it)
fix: cache `sid -> (username, created_at, last_seen)` in process for ~10 s and invalidate it from `revoke`/`revoke_others`/`delete` (single worker, so in-process invalidation is exact; the touch still writes at most once a minute); and drop `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` from `db.connect` after boot (set once in `ensure_schema`). Must keep: "log out everywhere" taking effect on the next request (the invalidation does that), the 250 ms touch timeout.

title: PRAC-72's missing compression is wider than the transfers page: every home poll and the cold static load ship uncompressed
what: PRAC-72 (open) names `/partials/transfers`. The same is true of every poll on the home page and of the static assets, which are 260 KB raw on a cold load (components.css 84 KB, htmx.min.js 48 KB, terminal.css 31 KB, cc.js 31 KB, ...).
cost: one visible admin home tab at 20 machines x 100 projects: home-transfers 33.5 KB every 2 s, fleet 75 KB / 15 s, queue 27 KB / 10 s, tree 83 KB / 30 s, problems 34 KB / 60 s = ~1.7 MB/min, ~2.4 GB/day for a wall display, vs ~55 KB/min gzipped (synthetic rows compress 20-50x; real HTML estimated 8-15x). At 500 projects the tree poll alone is 383 KB every 30 s.
evidence: `probe_builders.py` body vs `gzip.compress(body, 6)` sizes per route.
fix: PRAC-72's `GZipMiddleware(minimum_size=1024)` added as the OUTERMOST layer is safe on this Starlette (1.6): it already skips 206 responses, responses that carry Content-Encoding, and media/event-stream types, so the mounts' Range audio/video are untouched. Note one design choice for the owner: every page body carries the CSRF token beside some reflected query input (`?as=`, `?next=`), the BREACH precondition; the cheap answer is compressing `/static/` and `/partials/` only, or masking the token per response.

title: tab_memory.js saves the scroll position after every poll swap: a forced layout and two storage writes every ~2 s on a visible tab
where: `dashboard/static/tab_memory.js:345-348` (`htmx:afterSettle` -> `saveThrottled`), `256-265` (`save`: `querySelectorAll("details")`, `nearestSection` = `getBoundingClientRect` on every `h1-h4[id]`/`section[id]`, then `sessionStorage` + `localStorage` `setItem`); `166` (expired entries are skipped on read, never removed)
what: a poll never moves the reader, but every poll's settle runs a full save (throttled to one per 500 ms). On the home page that is every 2 s from the transfers poll alone.
cost: ~30 saves a minute on a visible home tab, ~43,000 a day on a wall display, each a synchronous layout read right after a swap plus two storage writes; on a phone (pwa.js slows the poll to 10 s) ~8,600 a day. Separately each `/project/<slug>` visited leaves a `ccsync.tab:` key in localStorage forever (at 500 projects, up to 500 stale keys; small but unbounded by time).
evidence: code read; poll cadences from `templates/fleet.html:77-119`.
fix: in the afterSettle handler, return early when the request was a poll (cc.js already has the `isPoll` test: `every`/`load` trigger, no user event); scroll, pagehide and visibilitychange still save. On `start()`, delete `ccsync.tab:` entries older than MAX_AGE_MS. Keeps CR-188's behaviour unchanged.

title: A video seek or an abandoned media request keeps streaming the rest of the file: /cards and /cards/edit never notice the browser has gone
where: dashboard/src/ccsync_dashboard/cards_wsgi.py:129-146; cards.py:803; cards_edit.py:701-726, 796-805; uvicorn httptools_impl.py:467-468; starlette middleware/base.py:204-241; MulticamPipeline cards/handler.py:1068-1095
what: uvicorn (ASGI spec 2.3) drops a send after the client disconnects without raising, and the BaseHTTPMiddleware stack has no disconnect listener, so the Cards handler's ConnectionError path never fires and cards_edit.Passthrough never stops. Every open-ended Range response runs to EOF with no back-pressure: the WSGI thread reads the vault file and pumps 64 KiB chunks through the event loop into the void; on /cards/edit httpx keeps pulling the Node child.
cost: Each <video>/<audio> seek or abort (several a second while scrubbing) reads the rest of the file: 300-700 MB for an hour-long 480p proxy, about 3,200 event-loop hops per 200 MB (0.44 s measured on this workstation, estimated 1-2 s per 500 MB on the NAS CPU), and holds one of the engine's 24 a2wsgi workers for an estimated 3-7 s, so a few seconds of scrubbing fills the pool and the page's JSON polls queue behind dead streams. Same bytes compete with lane B on the pool disks.
evidence: probe_disconnect.py: client read 256 KiB of a 200 MB bytes=0- response through five BaseHTTPMiddleware layers and closed; the a2wsgi+cards_wsgi producer produced 200.0 MiB (finished after 0.44 s) and the Passthrough producer 200.0 MiB (0.12 s). probe_disconnect_fix.py: with a GET-only disconnect listener the producer stopped at 0.4 MiB.
fix: Wrap the per-episode ASGI app (in CardsDispatch) and edit_proxy with a GET/HEAD-only task that awaits receive() for http.disconnect and sets an event; _Writer.write raises BrokenPipeError once set (the handler already closes on it), and the proxy stops aiter_raw() and acloses the upstream. Must ignore non-disconnect messages (body_size_gate's replay) and keep Range/206 bytes untouched.

title: Every /broll, /music and /sorter request opens a fresh SQLite connection on the event loop to ask is_admin (local accounts), ~69 ms beside any busy thread
what: The three async gates call auth.is_admin synchronously for every session request (thumbnails, media ranges, polls). Under DASH_AUTH_METHOD=local any name not in DASH_ADMIN_USERS costs db.connect (connect + 4 PRAGMAs) + SELECT + close on the event loop, and each sqlite3 call re-takes the GIL, waiting out the switch interval whenever a CPU-bound thread runs (the CR-351 effect on the loop thread).
cost: Measured 1.0 ms quiet, 68.7 ms beside one CPU-bound thread. A 60-thumbnail b-roll grid = about 4 s of the dashboard's event loop blocked for everyone while a Cards engine build, music index rebuild or AI worker runs. Today's studio is smb auth (no DB call), so it lands on the first local-accounts customer and every non-admin editor there.
evidence: probe_isadmin.py on a db.migrate'd temp DB, auth_method=local, non-listed user: quiet 1.008 ms, beside one CPU-bound thread 68.671 ms per call.
fix: Cache admin-ness per username for 5-10 s in process (cleared by the users routes on any role or disable change), or have login_gate stash it on request.state beside the session so the gates read it. Keep fail-closed; a demoted admin must lose the header within the TTL.

title: Gear identify keeps every earlier photo in the hot CLI conversation (quadratic input over 40 photos), and queued photos each hold a shared threadpool worker
what: Each photo is a further user turn, with its image, in one stream-json conversation that the CLI resends every turn, so turn n carries n images (MAX_TURNS 40). Each request also takes an anyio worker before waiting on the one-photo lock, for up to 120 s per photo ahead of it.
cost: A 40-photo session carries 820 image inputs instead of 40 (20.5x): an estimated ~1.3 M input tokens instead of ~64 k at ~1,600 tokens per photo, on the studio's Claude Code login; context and latency grow per turn against a 3.9 s warm-start saving. A burst of N photos holds N of the 40 shared threadpool workers (40 photos = /report and every sync route stall).
evidence: Read gear_ai.py; stream-json input keeps the conversation in the process (the reason the second turn is warm). Token figures estimated, no CLI run.
fix: Recycle the hot process after about 5 turns instead of 40, and take the lock before entering the threadpool (asyncio.Lock around run_in_threadpool) or 429 beyond a small queue. Keep one conversation at a time.

title: Nothing caps how many Claude Code CLI processes Timeline Cards starts inside the dashboard container
what: Runner.run is shared by every pooled engine and has no semaphore; each CLI-path call spawns a fresh Node claude process for the whole call. The engines choose their own parallelism and know nothing of each other or the container.
cost: Two open episodes, one translating (3) and one shortening (4), plus a search: 8-14 concurrent claude processes; at an estimated 150-300 MB RSS each, a 1.5-4 GB spike in the container that serves the fleet, beside two ~128 MB engines, with the dashboard a possible OOM victim.
evidence: Read as cited; per-process RSS estimated (no CLI run).
fix: A module-level BoundedSemaphore in Runner.run around the provider call (about 3 for the CLI path, higher for the SDK path), with time spent waiting counted against the call's timeout.

title: The SDK path builds a new Anthropic client (and connection pool) per call and never closes it
what: anthropic.Anthropic(api_key=key) is constructed per call and dropped, so each Cards AI call on the API path opens a new TCP+TLS connection and leaves an httpx pool for the GC.
cost: Hundreds of chunked translation calls per episode (estimated) each pay a fresh handshake (estimated 100-300 ms) a kept-alive client would not; sockets linger until GC. Small next to the LLM call.
evidence: Read as cited.
fix: Cache one client per key (rebuilt when the key changes), close it at shutdown.

title: A stop that lands between Popen and self._proc = proc leaves the new editor's child running and unflushed
what: stop() sets the flag then reads self._proc once; if the supervisor is between Popen returning and line 368, stop() sees no process, and _run then sees the flag and returns trusting stop() to terminate a child it never saw.
cost: The --write Node editor outlives the dashboard, its SIGTERM cut-list flush never runs, and a dashboard restarted in the same container starts a second writer on the same vault. Narrow window (a start in progress at shutdown, e.g. mid crash loop).
evidence: Read as cited.
fix: When _run's inner loop exits on _stop, terminate and wait for proc itself if alive (idempotent with stop()), or publish self._proc under _lock and have stop() read it under the same lock.

title: The AI provider resolver probes EVERY CLI, below the winner too, with no single-flight, on the request path
what: In AUTO, resolved() probes every CLI provider whose 600 s cache entry expired (two subprocesses each: --version and a real one-token call), although resolve_provider takes the first available and the lower probes can only change the reason string. probe_cli holds no lock across the spawn, so concurrent callers at expiry each spawn their own pair.
cost: Every 600 s of AI use the first Cards/ytdl/Settings call pays Claude Code's probe plus Codex's probe serially before its real call: measured 4 spawns per resolve (2 wasted), 32 spawns for 8 concurrent resolves. Estimated ~200 MB RSS per spawn of the 238 MB CLI, 5-20 s added latency warm and up to minutes cold, ~50 billed probe calls per CLI per working day, doubled with Codex installed.
evidence: probe_herd.py with stubbed _run: single resolve -> claude_code chosen, spawns claude_code --version 1, -p 1, codex --version 1, exec 1; 8 concurrent -> 32 spawns. No early exit in the PROVIDER_ORDER loop; _probe_lock guards only the dict.
ledger: new; related to ytdl-web-5 (pinned case only) and CR-121
fix: In AUTO probe in chain order and stop at the first available (rows below from unprobed_cli_state); per-provider lock in probe_cli so concurrent callers share one in-flight probe; optionally refresh the cache on a successful real call. Keep force=True, the pin refusal, CR-121 and CR-355 behaviour.

title: Every OTA apply copies every database twice, including a ~500 MB b-roll index it almost never migrates, and keeps up to eight such copies
what: apply copies dashboard.db, broll.db and music.db into staging/.dbcheck for stage-verify, then copies all three again into /data/backups/<ts>-before-<v>/ whether or not the new code migrates them. Per-version labels mean retention is 8 backups or 8 GiB.
cost: Per apply ~1 GB written for b-roll alone (2 x ~500 MB), estimated 10-20 s extra I/O on a NAS HDD pool; steady state ~4.2 GB of /data held (8 x ~520 MB) on the volume dashboard.db lives on; preflight's 2x-db free-space demand refuses updates earlier than needed at larger sites.
evidence: Code read (no branch skips an unmigrated DB); E: roll-queue roll.db = 501,460,992 bytes; music.db = 20,537,344 bytes.
fix: Have stage-verify report each DB's user_version before/after migrating its copy, and back up only the DBs whose version moved (always dashboard.db). Keep REL-10's backup_for_version, restore_backup and the preflight.

title: Interrupted downloads on the two UNATTENDED paths leave staging files that nothing sweeps
what: A kill during fetch_artifact_to leaves packages/<platform>/<file>.<uuid>.part (up to 200 MiB); the only sweeper runs inside the human PUT route, which a feed-only customer never calls. A kill mid-apply leaves code/<v>.tar.gz.part (never swept) and code/<v>.staging/ with ~520 MB of .dbcheck copies, removed only by a later apply's prune_code_trees; the healed state is 'failed' and auto-apply never retries a failed version.
cost: 0.2-0.8 GB of /data per interrupted fetch or apply, held indefinitely; rare but cumulative on the shell-less appliance.
evidence: Code read; _sweep_stale_parts has one call site (api.py:7703).
ledger: new; same shape as REL-15 (fixed for the CLI .staging)
fix: Sweep stale .part in publish_from_feed before downloading; in _heal_orphaned_progress, where the dead latch is cleared, remove code/*.tar.gz.part and code/*.staging.

title: The sign-in pty master fd is closed from two threads without the session lock, and while the reader thread may still read it
what: _kill reads and clears session._master without a lock; CANCEL runs it on the request thread while the worker loop runs it too, so both can close the same fd number, the second closing whatever reused it. The worker also closes the master after reader.join(timeout=2) while the reader may still loop on os.read(master). No wait() after proc.kill().
cost: Needs a CANCEL or timeout racing the child's exit, or a grandchild holding the slave; result is one stolen/closed descriptor in the dashboard process (an HTTP request or DB handle failing once). A few sign-ins per site per year.
evidence: Code read only; not reproduced.
fix: Swap the fd under session._lock and let only the reader close it on EOF/EIO; add proc.wait(timeout) after proc.kill().

title: The release runbook restarts the dashboard to force a feed check that a button already does, and soaking/staged records wait a whole poll interval
what: Pathway B step 5 says to docker restart the dashboard to trigger a feed check now; Check now (POST /api/v1/admin/feed/check) does the same without stopping Cards engines, the /cards/edit child and running ytdl jobs. The soak gates are re-evaluated only inside check_now, which runs daily.
cost: One avoidable container restart per studio release (estimated 10-60 s down plus lost in-flight work); on policy=current customer sites up to 24 h between a 30-minute soak ending and the build being offered (latency part PLAUSIBLE, depends on site policy).
evidence: Doc and code read.
fix: Point the runbook at Check now (or have publish_latest.py call the check route); re-run _apply_policy/apply_dashboard_policy hourly against the cached verified channel with no fetch and no re-verify.

title: Public share media requests re-resolve the whole folder on every request after an id-renumbering rebuild, and never heal
what: _member_id asks by the stored video_id while the page asks with the current id; after a renumbering rebuild they never match, so every poster/sprite/detail/proxy Range request falls back to public_video_ids = resolve_items over the whole folder. Nothing on the read path rewrites client_folder_items.video_id, so the slow path is permanent.
cost: 500-clip folder on the 50k index: 0.01 ms per card with ids intact vs 9.0 ms after renumbering; one page open = ~1,000 media requests = ~9 s of dashboard threadpool CPU and ~1M SQL statements, on every open and every Range request, on the anonymous Funnel door. Plus 0.35 ms ensure_schema and two SQLite connections per request.
evidence: p_share.py: all 500 _member_id calls 3 ms with ids intact, 4,594 ms with stored ids shifted.
fix: Heal on read: when resolve_items or the _member_id fallback resolves an item to a current id that is free in the folder, write it back to client_folder_items.video_id (the _rekey_stale_item move, best effort). Keep the per-request token/revoke and identity checks unchanged.

title: Every card downloads its full sprite sheet up front; the share page does it for the whole folder
what: The sprite overlay's background-image is set at card build time and hidden with opacity:0, which does not stop the fetch and cannot be lazy. Browse cards and share cards pull the whole sheet whether or not anyone hovers.
cost: Real sheets: median 58 KB, mean 215 KB, p90 613 KB, max 4.2 MB (posters 23 KB). A 24-card browse page ~5.2 MB of sprites vs ~0.55 MB of posters per render; a 500-clip share page ~107 MB on open over the Funnel.
evidence: Code read; sizes from ls -l of 12,101 sheets in E:\broll-queue\sprites (2.6 GB).
fix: Assign backgroundImage on first pointerenter inside wireSpriteScrub for browse and share cards; keep eager (or IntersectionObserver-deferred) loading only for search cards showing a static hit frame.

title: Semantic index rebuild peaks at ~3x the matrix in the dashboard process on every search_generation bump
what: _ensure_index fetchall()s every vector blob, then allocates and fills a new float32 matrix while the previous index is still referenced, so peak = old matrix + all blobs + new matrix + per-row tuples.
cost: 50k clips (274,950 rows): 422 MB matrix, 951 MB traced peak on a first build, ~1.37 GB on a rebuild, 4.0 s holding the lock. Today's 82,889 rows: est. ~290 MB first build, ~415 MB per rebuild, after every ingest/indexer write.
evidence: probe_search.py tracemalloc: cur/peak 473/951 MB, matrix 422 MB, build 4,046 ms at 50k; 42 MB / 95 MB at 5k.
fix: Iterate the cursor instead of fetchall, preallocate from the count already in the key, frombuffer into each row, drop the old index before building. Optionally store float16 after re-checking retrieval quality.

title: Per-search overhead: two COUNTs over embeddings, all visible ids into a Python set, a Python mask, before an 8 ms matmul
what: mode_availability runs COUNT(*) on embeddings on every /api/search (browse, keyword, pager) only to test non-zero; hybrid/semantic repeats it for the cache key, materialises every visible video id via _allowed_video_ids even with no user filter, and builds the mask with a Python generator over every embedding row. Paging re-runs the whole fused search.
cost: 50k clips: COUNT 25.9 ms, _allowed_video_ids 34.9 ms, mask 8.5 ms, matmul 8.3 ms; hybrid 117 ms, page 5 166 ms. Today est. ~30 ms per hybrid search and ~8 ms of COUNT per browse page.
evidence: probe_search.py component timings; EXPLAIN shows covering-index scan for COUNT, MAX(rowid) 0.0 ms.
fix: availability -> SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1; cache video_id/source columns as numpy arrays at build and mask with np.isin; precompute the BROWSE_PREDICATE-only mask per index key instead of re-querying.

title: Editor-side posters and sprites carry no Cache-Control, so every render revalidates every image
what: ETag only, no Cache-Control or Last-Modified, so the browser has no freshness and sends a conditional request per image per card render.
cost: 48 conditional round trips per 24-card render through the login gate and Tailscale, for files written once. Estimated tens to hundreds of ms per render remotely.
evidence: Header read; dashboard mount adds none (grep).
fix: Version editor-side URLs with ?v=<videos.hash>-<sprite_cells> and serve private, max-age=31536000, immutable; safe under renumbering since the version follows the clip. Leave /share/ media no-cache (MEDIA-22).

title: The detail route lists the archive folders twice per open
what: get_video calls insert_target_detail via _insert_target and again via _insert_object; each does two os.listdir calls with per-entry NFC normalisation.
cost: 4 listdirs instead of 2 per clip opened, each O(category folder size); proxy-tiers-3 warnings logged twice per open on an unreadable mount.
evidence: p_tree.py printed each warning twice for one get_video call.
fix: Compute insert_target_detail once in get_video, derive insert_share/insert_rel_path from it and pass it to _insert_object.

title: The ingest panel keeps polling at full rate in a background tab
what: Loopback 1.5 s, batch 5 s, list 10 s polls run while the panel is open with no visibilitychange handling.
cost: Per hidden hour: 2,400 calls into the editor's tray and up to 1,080 dashboard SQLite reads, for as long as the tab stays open.
evidence: No document.hidden or visibilitychange in ingest.js or app.js.
fix: Pause list/server polls when hidden and stretch or stop the loopback poll when no upload is running; poll once on becoming visible. Uploads are XHR-driven and unaffected.

title: style.css exists three times (b-roll, music, ytdl), ~70% shared; the client viewer loads the whole editor sheet
what: 915/1,282 of music's and 884/1,299 of ytdl's distinct lines also appear in b-roll's sheet; each is served no-cache; the public share page pulls the 94 KB editor sheet.
cost: ~165 KB of near-duplicate CSS shipped and revalidated, three edit sites per shared rule.
evidence: comm -12 over sorted unique lines; file sizes 94/71/75 KB.
fix: One shared base sheet served by the dashboard plus small per-app sheets; a trimmed sheet for the share viewer. Keep document-relative URLs and the SHARE_ASSETS allow-list.

title: Frames now come from the 1080p proxy at full size: about twice the local VLM's image tokens, and 8- and 9-frame windows go past the 16k context
where: broll/indexer/broll_index/ffmpeg_tools.py:821 (extract_frames, no scale); pipeline.py:211 (_frames_source); ffmpeg_tools.py:312 (PROXY_HEIGHT 1080); local_vlm.py:46-47; config.py:255
what: The local backend was tuned on 960x540 frames (~1,024 tokens each after the minimum). Since 2026-09-17 frames are cut from the 1080p proxy at native size, ~2,040 Qwen3-VL tokens each, so a 9-frame window is ~18.4k+1k tokens against a 16,384-token slot.
cost: Every clip whose balanced window has 8-9 frames (e.g. 8-9 or 15-18 frames, ~30-36 s or 60-72 s at max_gap 4 s) gets HTTP 400, raised as LocalVlmError, which matches no fatal marker, so the clip is marked 'error' and the queue moves on. Even if capped: ~2x encode_ms (2.7 s -> ~5.4 s per 7-frame window), and 3.2x JPEG bytes per frame on 401k+ kept frames.
evidence: usage.jsonl: 7 frames = 8,473 / 8 frames = 9,531 input tokens at 960x540; server log n_ctx_slot 16384, --image-min-tokens 1024; video 25438 frames 960x540, proxy and newest proxies 1920x1080; last local run predates the 1080p re-encode; probe 99 vs 31 KiB/frame. Model not loaded (brief rule).
fix: Scale frames in extract_frames (-vf scale='min(960,iw)':-2) so frames match the eval regardless of proxy height; keep the (timestamp,path) pairing. Optionally treat 'exceeds the available context' as run-fatal.

title: The packet count that costs a second full NAS read of every original is already printed by the proxy encode
what: _bad() demuxes the whole original over SMB (ffprobe -count_packets) for the exact frame check; the encode already reads every source packet, and at -loglevel verbose prints 'Input stream #0:0 (video): N packets read'. The verify decode likewise prints dest packets and decode errors. The source is also ffprobed 3 times per clip.
cost: Per clip: ~200 MB extra read (~4.3 s at 46 MB/s); ~6-8 h of NAS read per back-catalogue pass of 5-7k clips, ~60 h at 50k (estimated), shared across the parallel_local workers.
evidence: Probe: verbose encode summary '1800 packets read; 1800 frames decoded; 0 decode errors' equals ffprobe nb_read_packets 1800 on the same file.
ledger: related to CR-286B / broll-indexer-1 (fixed; names 'a count carried forward' as the way back)
fix: Parse src/dst counts and decode errors from the encode and verify passes' verbose summaries; keep frames_match exact and 'both known or skip'; change the companion twin and parity tests in the same commit; count_frames_cmd as fallback.

title: The API describe path never hits the prompt cache: the ~3k-token instruction block sits after the images, with the per-window sheet list near its top
what: Every call is [4 images][prompt]; the images and the sheet list (line 12 of 226) vary per window, so no stable prefix exists and no cache_control is set.
cost: ~2 calls/clip, ~10k calls per 5k-clip archive; ~2.7k of ~7k input tokens could bill at 0.1x, ~35-40% of input spend (~$50 per 10k calls on sonnet-5, estimated). The Haiku 4.5 minimum is 4,096 tokens, so it caches only if the prefix clears that.
evidence: Code read: no system block or cache_control anywhere in broll/indexer.
fix: Put the fixed instructions plus taxonomy in a system block with cache_control; keep images then the sheet list in the user turn; verify cache_read_input_tokens > 0 on the second call.

title: Offline backfill pays full price: the Message Batches API (half price) is not used
what: The overnight API stage drives synchronous calls through workers, semaphores and rate-limit sleeps; the Batches API does the same work asynchronously at 50% of the token price.
cost: Anthropic backend only (opt-in): ~$0.02-0.03 saved per call, ~$200-300 per 10k calls (estimated), stacking with caching.
evidence: Code read; no batches usage.
fix: Add a --batch mode: custom_id video:window, submit, poll, merge per video, write as now; clips stay 'proxied' until complete.

title: anthropic.max_tokens 8000 sits below a third of the archive's historical outputs; a truncated answer costs two paid calls and then marks the clip error
what: stop_reason max_tokens only logs; the truncated JSON fails to parse, the window is re-asked at the same ceiling (paid twice), then the clip is marked error. Unused headroom is free.
cost: Historical haiku output: median 5,961, p90 12,783, p99 20,313; 2,915/8,996 (32%) over 8,000 - if visible output rather than CLI thinking, ~1/3 of windows truncate.
evidence: Distribution computed from E:\broll-queue\usage.jsonl (CLI era).
fix: Default to 16000; on max_tokens retry once with a doubled ceiling.

title: The cost estimate and alias table lag the price list: sonnet-5 is costed 50% high
what: PRICE_PER_MTOK has claude-sonnet-5 at $3/$15; the current price is $2/$10. Current-generation models are absent from the alias table.
cost: Every usage.jsonl forecast for the default model overstates cost by 50%.
evidence: Code read against the current model/price table.
fix: Correct the row and add current models; update the doc table in the same change.

title: usage.jsonl takes concurrent appends without a lock; the live file has a torn line, and the documented forecast snippet crashes on it
what: N threads (and a second --after-id process) open-append per call; one line in the live file is the fragment 'n_ms": 25423}', and the doc's json.loads-per-line forecast raises on it.
cost: 1 torn line of 12,705; the recommended forecast fails outright until the file is hand-edited.
evidence: My parse of the live usage.jsonl failed at line 8716.
fix: Single os.write per record on an O_APPEND fd under a lock; make the snippet skip bad lines.

title: An account-wide stop in the middle of a clip throws away the windows already paid for
what: Window results live only in memory until the final write; FatalRunError on window k drops windows 1..k-1 and the rerun pays for them again.
cost: Up to (windows-1) calls per in-flight clip per stop; tens of calls on a night of repeated limits (estimated).
evidence: Code read.
fix: Persist each parsed window as sheets/<id>/window_<k>.json keyed by sheets and model; reuse on rerun; delete after the write.

title: A rescan writes and commits every unchanged file
what: A known, same-size file still goes through upsert_video: a second lookup, an UPDATE with identical values and a commit.
cost: 1.12 ms/file measured: ~5 s per 4,482-file share, ~9 min per 500k files of pure commits.
evidence: probe_scan.py, 5,000 rows, WAL.
fix: Skip the write when hash/size/in_inbox already match; batch the rest per directory or per 500 rows.

title: A music sweep with nothing changed still loads CLAP onto the GPU and re-scores the whole library
what: The full sweep loads the CLAP model before computing todo and always retags; the --queue path already skips the retag when nothing was added.
cost: Per manual sweep: seconds of model load, ~1 GB VRAM beside Resolve, and a whole-library rescore for zero changes.
evidence: Code read.
fix: Compute todo first; with nothing to analyse, prune or close, exit before loading CLAP.

title: An open /music tab spawns a Resolve worker child on the editor's machine every 30 s, forever
where: music/web/static/app.js:1032 (`setInterval(refreshResolveStatus, 30000)`), app.js:424-441; companion music_server.py:221 (`PROBE_TTL_S = 3.0`), :297-306, :156-200 (`call` = `subprocess.run` of the frozen exe as a worker)
what: The status dot polls `GET 127.0.0.1:8899/music/status` every 30 s from page load until the tab closes, with no visibility check and regardless of whether a player pane is open. Each call is answered by `cached_probe`, whose TTL is 3 s, so every 30 s tick misses the cache and `subprocess.run`s the companion exe re-entered as a Resolve worker that calls `resolve_bridge.connect()`.
cost: 120 child processes per hour per open music tab (hidden tabs are throttled to ~1/min by Chrome, so still ~60/h), each a frozen-companion start (CR-107's own note: ~80 MB each; PRAC-77: the exe is onefile) plus one scripting connection to fuscript, on the machine whose CPU/RAM Resolve needs. An editor who leaves the music page open in a tab all day = ~500-1,000 worker spawns for a dot nobody is looking at. Measured: the cadence and TTL by reading; per-spawn cost estimated from CR-107/PRAC-77 (not measured, the live companion is off limits).
evidence: app.js has no `visibilitychange`/`document.hidden` anywhere; `refreshResolveStatus` is also called after every send (app.js:387), the only time the answer matters.
ledger: related to CR-107 (fixed the burst of probes, not the steady cadence); related to PRAC-77 (open)
fix: Poll only while the document is visible AND a player pane is open (start on `openPane`, stop on `closePane`/`visibilitychange`), keeping the post-send refresh; optionally have the companion answer `/music/status` from its in-process Resolve watcher state instead of a child. Must not break: the CR-68 rule (one `scriptapp()` caller) and the CR-107 single-flight slot.

title: Fleet-ingested tracks never get a preview proxy, so every preview streams the ~60 MB original, and replays re-download it
where: musicweb/routes_media.py:82-103 (`audio_source`), :145-179 (206 path); server/install_dashboard_app.py:3610 (`music-proxies:/music-proxies:ro`); musicweb/routes_fleet.py (no proxy route); music/web/DEPLOY.md:202
what: A proxy is used only if `<PROXIES_DIR>/<id>.mp3` exists. That directory is a read-only bind filled by a base-rig push, and neither the fleet ingest path (companion -> `/batches/.../result` + `uploaded`) nor the container creates one, so every track added through the companion since 2026-08-18 previews from its original. Browsers always open `<audio>` with `Range: bytes=0-`, which goes down the StreamingResponse branch, which sends no `ETag`/`Last-Modified`/`Cache-Control`, so nothing about the response is reusable and a second click re-fetches it.
cost: DEPLOY.md's own figure is "streams the 60 MB originals over Tailscale"; a 128k proxy of the same 4-min cue is ~3.8 MB, so ~15x the bytes per preview for every fleet-added track, every time it is clicked, to every remote editor, until someone re-runs make_proxies on the base rig and re-pushes 864+ MB. At commercial scale (no GPU base rig, bug-music-5) that is never.
evidence: grep: no writer of `proxy_path` outside the base-rig indexer; the bind is `:ro`; `chunks()` response headers carry only Accept-Ranges/Content-Length/Content-Range/X-Audio-Source.
ledger: new (related to bug-music-5, open; bug-music-7 is about stale proxies, not missing ones)
fix: Have the companion (which already runs ffmpeg for the .ogg transcode) upload a 128k proxy beside the original, or let the container's ffmpeg build one into a writable proxies dir on first `uploaded`; and add a strong `ETag` (size+mtime_ns+id) and `Cache-Control: private, max-age=86400` to both audio branches so a replay is a cache hit. Must keep the rule that a Range is never answered from the other file (proxy vs original) and the id-reuse guard (music-4: the ETag must include mtime/size).

title: The ONNX text tower holds ~560 MB in the dashboard process for its whole life after one search
where: musicweb/search.py:176-188 (`shared_encoder`, module global, never released); text_encoder.py:242-268
what: The encoder is lazy (good: import of `musicweb.search` costs 0.10 s and ~30 MB, dashboard boot is unaffected), but once any editor runs one text search the ~500 MB fp32 InferenceSession stays resident in the single dashboard process until restart; there is no idle unload. Music search is an occasional, bursty activity.
cost: Measured with the real artefact: working set 31 MB -> 592 MB after load (peak 744 MB during load), cold load 0.67 s (warm file cache), 9.2 ms per query. So one search a week pins ~560 MB for the week, in the container that also runs the fleet dashboard, Cards engines and b-roll's semantic index. On a small NAS (8-16 GB, ZFS ARC) that is the largest single resident consumer music adds.
evidence: `probe_encoder.py` output: `import musicweb.search: 0.10 s ws 31.5 MB`; `cold load 0.67 s ws 592 MB private 1344 MB peak 744 MB`; `median of 40 9.2 ms`.
ledger: new (bug-music-2's fix list suggests pre-warming at mount, which would make this unconditional - do not)
fix: Drop `_encoder` after N minutes without a query (a timestamp checked under `_encoder_lock` by the next search, or a single daemon timer), accepting a ~0.7-2 s first query after idle; optionally try `SessionOptions.enable_cpu_mem_arena = False`. Must keep MUSIC-5/MUSIC-8 single-flight (one load under the lock) and must not unload while a request holds the reference (callers keep the object they got, so dropping the global is safe).

title: The search index costs ~27 KB/track resident and ~2x that on every rebuild: 1.34 GB held and 2.84 GB peak at 50k tracks, with no single-flight
where: musicweb/db.py:337-358 (`load_matrix`, `load_window_matrix`: `fetchall()` then `np.stack` of per-row `frombuffer`); search.py:24-41, 257-270 (`refresh` builds outside the lock, no in-flight guard); routes_fleet.py:133-148, 251-254, 172
what: Up to 12 window vectors per track are held as one float32 matrix (12 x 512 x 4 B = 24 KB/track) plus the track matrix. The loaders materialise every row as a Python `sqlite3.Row` with its blob before stacking, so the build peaks at ~2.1x the result, and `refresh()` builds a NEW index while the old one is still live (another +1x). Nothing stops two refreshes at once: a fleet `result` refresh, `_settle_scores` at release, a search tripping `_looks_stale`, and `/api/reload` all build independently.
cost: Measured on synthetic DBs: 5k tracks: build 0.76 s, held 134 MB, peak 284 MB. 50k tracks: build 8.2 s, held 1,342 MB, peak 2,843 MB (plus the old index still referenced -> ~4.2 GB transient in the worst case, more if two builds overlap). Today's ~400 tracks: ~11 MB, harmless. A commercial customer with a 50k-cue production library would OOM a small NAS on the first fleet ingest batch. bug-music-6 (open) means every heartbeat-induced rebuild pays this too.
evidence: `probe_index.py`: `Index build 8.18 s; held 1342 MB, peak during build 2843 MB; win_mat 1229 MB track_mat 102 MB`.
ledger: related to bug-music-6 (open; the revision-counter fix there removes most rebuilds but not the size) and PL-RES-75 (b-roll's twin, which says "check the music CLAP index too" - this is that check)
fix: Fill a preallocated array from a streaming cursor (`SELECT COUNT(*)` then `np.empty((n, d))` and copy row by row: peak ~= held); serialise `refresh` behind one in-flight lock that later callers wait on instead of building again; consider float16 storage for `win_mat` (halves it; verify top-k on the eval set first). Append-only for a single fleet result is the bigger win but needs the delete path (prune, `_drop_unlanded_tracks`) to force a full rebuild.
risk: low risk (streaming + single-flight), medium (float16, needs the eval)

title: Text search pools window scores in a Python loop: 4x slower than numpy at scale
what: After one matmul, `pool='max'` walks every window in Python (`for tid, s in zip(...)` with a dict update) and `pool='mean'` does the same per track, then sorts the whole dict to take 60.
cost: Per search (every editor query and every filter change under a query). Measured: 5k tracks: 10 ms (max) / 2 ms (mean) vs 3.2 ms vectorised; 50k tracks: 108 ms / 25 ms vs 26.3 ms vectorised, of which 22.7 ms is the matmul itself. The loop is ~80 ms of GIL-holding Python per query on the dashboard's single worker at 50k. Negligible today (~400 tracks).
evidence: `probe_index.py`; the vectorised version (`np.maximum.reduceat` over `win_tids` boundaries, which are sorted by `ORDER BY track_id, idx`, then `argpartition` for k) returned the identical top-60 ids.
fix: Replace both loops with reduceat + argpartition; keep the ids as Python ints on the way out (the comment at :113-115 about numpy int64 binding still applies).

title: An open player pane redraws the waveform and rewrites two DOM nodes 60 times a second, even when paused
what: `tick` re-arms `requestAnimationFrame` unconditionally while `state.playing === t.id`, so a pane left open on a paused track repaints the whole canvas (clear + one `fillRect` per 3 px of width) and assigns `time.textContent` and `pbtn.textContent` every frame, which invalidates layout each frame.
cost: 60 wakeups/s (120 on a 120 Hz monitor) for as long as the tab is visible with a pane open, typically on the editor's second monitor beside Resolve. Estimated well under 1 ms CPU per frame, but it keeps the compositor and the GPU awake for a paused player. Hidden tabs stop rAF, so the cost is bounded to visible time.
evidence: code reading; nothing in `tick` checks `a.paused`.
fix: Run the loop only between `play` and `pause`/`ended` events (start on `playing`, stop on `pause`), and paint once on seek/resize/peaks arrival as it already does; write the text nodes only when the displayed second changes.

title: The SPA's 205 KB of static files are re-read from disk and re-sent uncompressed on every /music load
what: Each static route `read_text()`s the file per request and returns a bare `Response` with no `ETag`, `Last-Modified` or `Cache-Control`, and the dashboard has no gzip middleware (PRAC-72), so every page load downloads app.js 44 KB + ingest.js 62 KB + style.css 71 KB + cc_spa.js 14 KB + index.html 13 KB = 205 KB. `/api/peaks/{id}` (900 bytes, immutable for an id until a prune) is also uncached, so reopening a track refetches it after a reload.
cost: Per /music page load per editor: ~205 KB over Tailscale and 5 file reads on the single worker; with validators it would be 5 x 304s (~2 KB). Small per load, but it is the whole SPA every time.
evidence: code reading; `wc -c static/*`.
fix: Serve these five through the dashboard's `static_files.py` pattern (validators + `Cache-Control: no-cache`), or add an ETag from mtime+size; keep the document-relative URLs and the pinned content types (tests/test_mounted_prefix.py, test_api.py). Give peaks a `private, max-age` + ETag that includes the row's track rel_path or a hash, so music-4's id reuse cannot serve a stale waveform.

title: Every metadata read scans the tracks table with its 2 KB embedding inline, and browse sorts without an index
where: schema.sql:16-37 (`tracks.embedding BLOB` inline), routes_api.py:57-100 (`stats`: 3 scans; `facets`: SUM over tracks), :180-206 (`tracks`: `ORDER BY t.filename` / `t.analyzed_at`)
what: The 2 KB vector lives in every `tracks` row, so `COUNT(*)`, `SUM(duration)`, `SUM(bytes)`, `SUM(bpm IS NULL)` and the browse scan all read every vector page; browse uses a temp B-tree (EXPLAIN: `SCAN t` + `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY`) because `filename` and `analyzed_at` have no index.
cost: Each page load runs stats + facets + tracks. Measured: 5k tracks 8 / 9 / 11 ms; 50k tracks 93 / 94 / 101 ms (newest: 146 ms), i.e. ~290 ms of single-worker time per /music page load at 50k, and again after every batch completion (`refreshLibrary`).
evidence: `probe_routes.py` output and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.
fix: Cheapest safe step: one aggregate query for stats, plus covering indexes `tracks(filename)` and `tracks(analyzed_at)` (and `(duration, bytes, bpm)` for the sums) in schema.sql, which is CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS and needs no migration. Moving the embedding out of `tracks` is the real fix but is a migration the indexer shares.
risk: low risk (indexes) / M, medium (moving the column)

title: The ingest-batch lease machinery exists twice (music and b-roll) and is kept in step by hand
where: music/web/musicweb/ingest_batches.py (1,336 lines) vs broll/web/app/ingest_batches.py (1,410 lines); music/web/static/ingest.js (1,543) vs broll/web/static/ingest.js (1,963)
what: 29 functions share a name; 11 are byte-identical after stripping docstrings (`lease_live`, `heartbeat`, `_check_transition`, `new_uid`, `set_upload_paused`, ...), and the lease/cancel/expiry set (`expire_stale_leases`, `cancel`, `cancel_requested_for`, `retry_failed`, `_recount`, `list_batches`) differs only in log text, type hints and the b-roll-only `proxies_live` state. The ledger shows fixes landing as "twins" (music-1's twin, bug-broll-4 music twin, bug-music-ytdl-2). They have NOT drifted in behaviour today (the 2026-09-18b cancelled-lease fix is in both). The two ingest.js files share 43 function names but only 29% of their lines, so they have already diverged and are not worth merging.
cost: Every lease/claim/cancel fix is two edits, two test files and two reviews; the ~300 lines of lease code are where three twin fixes have already been needed. Saving: ~300 lines and one class of "fixed on one side" bug.
evidence: AST diff of the 29 same-named functions (scratch `ingest_batches` comparison).
fix: Only if a third ingest kind arrives: lift the lease state machine (lease_live, heartbeat, expire_stale_leases, cancel*, _check_transition, now_iso/_parse_iso, new_uid) into one stdlib-only module vendored into both trees with a test that pins the two copies byte-equal, rather than a shared import (the two apps deploy separately and `app` vs `musicweb` packaging is load-bearing per CLAUDE.md).

title: The ingest ledger is never pruned, and the name checks scan all of it on every result
where: musicweb/ingest_batches.py:360-366 (`reserved_names`), :963 (called per item `result`), :493 (per precheck); db.py:557-578 (`_name_promised`, `lower(dest_name)` per candidate x 3 spellings)
what: Nothing deletes `ingest_batches`/`ingest_items` rows. `reserved_names` is documented as "every name an unlanded item has already been promised" but its filter keeps `live` items (landed for good), so it returns every name ever ingested; `lower(dest_name)` defeats any index.
cost: Measured at 100,000 ledger rows: `reserved_names` 54 ms per call, `_name_promised` 11.8 ms per candidate (x up to 3 spellings, x collisions). One `reserved_names` runs per item result, so a 500-track drop at that ledger size spends ~27 s of single-worker time on it. Today's ledger is hundreds of rows: negligible; 100k rows is several years of a 20-editor customer.
evidence: `probe_ledger.py`.
fix: Add `'live'` to the excluded states in both places (a landed name is already covered by the `tracks` and disk checks; confirm with the music-3 / bug-music-ytdl-2 tests) and add a partial expression index `ON ingest_items(lower(dest_name)) WHERE state NOT IN (...)`; optionally age out terminal batches older than N months.

title: A live stream wedges the fleet-wide server worker with no bound (pasted /live/ link, or a ticked live result)
what: The server executor downloads whatever the URL resolves to with no live-stream refusal and no wall-clock limit, and the worker reads cancel_requested only between clips. parse_url_list accepts /live/ links, a paste never passes the filter phase, and a search job's 'live or no duration' drop is a soft deselect the editor can overrule. yt-dlp records an ongoing live stream until it ends.
cost: One pasted 24/7 /live/ link holds the single fleet-wide worker indefinitely: every editor's jobs queue behind it, a .part grows ~3-4 GB/hour at 1080p (estimated) on the NAS, CANCEL is not read until the clip ends, and a container restart re-attaches (reset_stale_jobs keeps downloading jobs pending) unless cancel was pressed first. The companion is bounded by CLIP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 2 h; the server is not.
evidence: Read build_opts/download (no match_filter, no is_live check), _ID_PATHS includes 'live', _phase_download checks cancel/lease only per iteration, companion ytdl_executor.py:324 CLIP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS. Not run against YouTube per the brief.
fix: Refuse live/upcoming in build_opts via a match_filter (!is_live & live_status != is_upcoming) with a clip-row note, and add a per-clip deadline plus a cancel check that aborts from the progress hook on the worker thread so the abort follows the normal _record_failure cleanup path; keeps the 'never torn down from another thread' rule.

title: The two executors' conversion step has drifted: the server's ffmpeg/ffprobe have no timeout and cannot be cancelled
what: The companion's edit-ready conversion uses Popen, a 3 h ceiling, a cancellable child and a tree kill; the server's vendored copy runs a blocking subprocess.run with no timeout, so a hung or very slow libx264 re-encode or ffprobe holds the single fleet-wide worker and a cancel waits for it. The encode runs in the dashboard container at full thread count with no nice/-threads cap.
cost: Every 1440p/2160p clip (VP9/AV1 only above 1080p) is a full crf-18 medium re-encode on the NAS CPU, tens of minutes per clip-hour (estimated); the worker is unavailable to every editor meanwhile, cancel is not honoured, and dashboard requests compete for CPU. A wedged ffmpeg is a worker wedged until restart.
evidence: Read both implementations side by side; ytdl_common is already the shared contract module and carries neither timeout.
fix: Move CLIP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS/CONVERT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS into ytdl_common for both sides; run the server's ffmpeg via Popen with a poll loop that also checks a cancel callable, kill on either, and reuse the existing unstage() failure path. Optionally cap -threads so the dashboard keeps a core.

title: Every download-phase poll re-fetches the whole manifest (296 KB for 400 candidates) to draw 40 rows, uncompressed, in hidden tabs too
what: While a job downloads, each tick fetches the 7 KB poll plus the full manifest (every candidate and column) only to read dl_state/dl_error of the selected rows. No visibilitychange handling anywhere in the SPA and no response gzip.
cost: Measured 296,156 bytes per manifest (400 candidates, 40 selected). A 30-minute 40-clip download at 5 s ticks = ~360 fetches = ~107 MB per open tab per job, over the tailnet for remote editors; doubles with a second or forgotten background tab.
evidence: Probe: real schema in a temp DB, manifest body built exactly as routes_api.manifest builds it (3.3 ms, 296 KB); read poll() and renderDownloads.
fix: Carry the dl_state != 'none' rows (about 6 KB for 40) in the poll response while downloading and drop the per-tick manifest fetch; keep the terminal-phase loadManifest. Skip or stretch ticks while document.hidden.

title: The poll never stops at terms_review and re-renders the checkbox list every tick
what: terms_review is a person-wait phase like ready_for_review, but polling continues at 5 s for as long as the tab is open and each tick rebuilds every checkbox row, losing keyboard focus and risking a click on a detached node.
cost: A review left open overnight is ~17,000 requests per tab per day, each 5-6 SQL statements on the dashboard's single process; ~350k/day at 20 editors with a parked tab each (estimated).
evidence: Read poll() stop set and renderTermReview.
fix: Stop polling at terms_review (the continue action can reschedule) or slow it to 30 s; render the list once per job and update only the count afterwards.

title: Filter and enrich phases commit once per row (927 ms vs 11 ms for 400 rows)
what: Every row write in the filter phase (which shows no per-row progress) is its own WAL commit and fsync.
cost: Measured 927 ms for 400 per-row commits vs 11 ms in one transaction on NVMe; slower on ZFS with sync writes, and 400 write-lock acquisitions contend with select clicks. Once per search.
evidence: Probe against the real schema in a temp DB.
fix: Wrap each filter sub-step in one transaction via a non-committing set_video variant; keep per-chunk enrich commits and committed phase transitions.

title: Each review-grid checkbox click rebuilds the whole grid twice
what: toggle() calls renderGrid() optimistically and again on the reply; renderGrid empties #grid and recreates every visible card with a new img.
cost: Up to 400 cards (~2,400 nodes, 400 images) rebuilt twice per click; estimated 10-40 ms per rebuild; curating 100 clips is 200 full rebuilds with thumbnail re-decodes, on a laptop beside Resolve.
evidence: Read; not measured in a browser.
fix: Update only the clicked card and the footer/header counts; keep renderGrid for filter, chip and bulk changes.

title: Search candidates are kept forever: job_videos / job_video_terms are never pruned
where: ytdl/web/schema.sql:208-258; db.py (no DELETE outside boot recovery, erase, _drop_forgotten_terms)
what: Every candidate of every search stays in ytdl.db after the job is done; nothing reads jobs older than the 20-job Recent list except a deep link.
cost: Measured 356 KB for one 400-candidate job; ~2 searches/day today = ~250 MB/year, ~2 GB/year at 20 editors and ~15 searches/day, in a DB the container holds open and snapshots copy.
evidence: Probe DB size; grep of DELETE statements in db.py.
fix: In the retention pass that item asks for, drop job_videos/job_video_terms of terminal jobs older than N days, keeping the jobs row and never touching the downloads ledger; manifest.json already keeps download provenance.

title: Pre-op snapshots (ccsync-pre-*) never expire, so nothing deleted after one is ever freed
where: server/common.py:2406; server/backends/truenas.py:955-989; server/backends/synology.py:1241-1271; server/setup_tree.py:288; server/setup_snapshots.py; docs/BACKUP_RESTORE.md:116
what: Every setup_tree run snapshots the whole tree dataset and every deploy the apps dataset as ccsync-pre-<label>-<ts>; nothing in the repo ever destroys a ccsync-pre-* snapshot (the runbook says 'until the pool prunes them by hand'). A snapshot pins every block deleted after it. On DSM the description is the bare label, so the backends have drifted and DSM pre-op snapshots cannot be identified.
cost: Once per new project (~100 today, 500 at scale) plus several deploys a week. Deleting a finished 1-2 TB project frees nothing while any older pre-op snapshot exists; on the apps dataset each deploy pins app.old trees, music artefacts (up to 1.4 GB), backup rotations and dashboard.db churn - estimated several GB/month, unbounded.
evidence: grep of server/, dashboard/src, companion/src, tools/ for zfs destroy / pool.snapshot.delete / ccsync-pre: only the creator; BACKUP_RESTORE.md retention row; KNOWN_BUGS.md:10233 and :30084 name live pre-op snapshots; synology.py:1263 passes desc=label while truenas delegates to snapshot_now with the prefixed name.
ledger: new (related to PL-RES-109 (open), which concerns the expiring scheduled snapshots)
fix: In snapshot_before (same ssh call as the zfs snapshot) or as a setup_snapshots --apply step, destroy <dataset>@ccsync-pre-* older than 30 days, never the newest per label, never one marked ccsync:keep. On DSM pass the ccsync-pre-<label>-<ts> name as the description (synology.snapshot delegating to snapshot_now).

title: check_health.py dies with a traceback when the NAS is unreachable, skipping every later check
what: check_tailscale (via container_exec -> run_ssh), check_tree (run_ssh) and check_editor_accounts (truenas_api -> requests.ConnectionError) are unguarded; cli() only catches EnvError/NotImplementedError. The script's own 'a health check must not crash on the thing it is checking' rule is applied to Syncthing and the dashboard only.
cost: Exactly when something is down: traceback after check 1, checks 2b-7 (local tailnet path, Syncthing, SFTP transport, dashboard) never run, exit 1, which the documented contract reads as 'one check failed'. setup_tree prints a traceback and no snapshot verdict on a dropped channel.
evidence: Probe with a scratch site.toml, TRUENAS_HOST=127.0.0.1, CCSYNC_SSH_PORT=59999 (nothing listening), pinned throwaway key: NoValidConnectionsError raised from check_health.py:613 -> truenas.py:151 -> common.py:1542, exit 1.
fix: Run each check through a wrapper turning any exception into report(False, '<check>: could not run (...)') and continue; use run_ssh_guarded or catch in setup_tree/write_marker so a dropped channel ends in a FAILED line plus snapshot_verdict().

title: publish_db on Synology runs the swap without the DSM PATH, so docker exec / synoacltool are not found and every publish is refused
what: synology.py states docker and the syno CLIs are not on sudo's PATH on stock DSM, hence backend.root_cmd (PATH_EXPORT + sudo /bin/sh -c). publish_db hand-builds 'sudo -S sh -c <swap>' instead; the swap's integrity step runs docker exec ... python3 and falls back to a host python3 DSM does not have, and synoacltool -copy fails too (non-fatal).
cost: Every publish_db --which broll --apply on a Synology site exits 11 at quick_check (live index safe, but the index can never be published); --no-integrity-check gets past it but leaves the new file without its ACL copied, so the container may be unable to write ingest rows or the file is world-writable under internal-sftp -u 000.
evidence: publish_db.py:947/:676 vs synology.py:185-186; the counts/drain calls work on DSM because they go through container_exec -> _root -> root_cmd (synology.py:372-374); no server test renders the swap through a Synology backend. Code read only, not run on DSM.
fix: Use backend.root_cmd(swap) when the backend has one, else the current TrueNAS string (byte-identical there); add a test asserting PATH_EXPORT precedes docker exec in the Synology swap.

title: The Syncthing API key and GUI password are taken on the command line, and the runbook tells operators to type them there
what: Four scripts accept --api-key (and secure_syncthing_gui --password) as argv, and three runbook lines put '--api-key <syncthing-api-key>' on the command line, against the repo's own never-on-a-command-line rule; load_secrets.ps1 already provides SYNCTHING_API_KEY.
cost: Once per editor onboarding and per hand-provisioned project the key lands in PSReadLine's plaintext ConsoleHost_history.txt (kept indefinitely) and the process list. The key is full control of the NAS Syncthing: share any folder with any device, i.e. the whole tree.
evidence: argparse lines and SERVER.md lines above; docs/SECRETS.md lists SYNCTHING_API_KEY as a DPAPI-managed secret.
fix: Rewrite the runbook lines to rely on the environment after load_secrets.ps1; keep --api-key for compatibility but warn when used; read the GUI password via getpass/env rather than argv.

title: One full SSH connect + password auth per remote command: 7 handshakes for a b-roll publish, 3 for a new project, one redundant
what: run_ssh opens and closes a paramiko client per call. publish_db --which broll --apply = 7 connections on TrueNAS (8 on DSM); setup_tree = 3. The separate 'wc -c' check duplicates the swap script's own size check on the .new copy.
cost: Estimated 0.3-0.6 s per handshake on LAN, 1-2 s over a relayed tailnet: ~2-4 s per publish locally, up to ~14 s relayed, against a measured 4 s local half; one NAS auth-log entry per call.
evidence: Call sites listed; truenas_rpc.py:543-612 already pools its session for the same reason.
fix: Cache one connected client per (host, port, user) for the process lifetime, reconnecting once if the transport died; keep password-on-stdin per command and the host-key policy. Drop the standalone wc -c round trip.

title: run_ssh reads stdout to EOF before stderr: more than 2 MiB of stderr wedges the call until the inactivity timeout
what: paramiko's 2 MiB channel window is shared by stdout and stderr and only replenished on read; unread stderr past 2 MiB blocks the remote writer, stdout never reaches EOF, and the call waits for the 120 s inactivity timeout then raises.
cost: A setup_tree re-run over an existing 20k+ file project on a dataset refusing ownership changes (per-file chown errors, ~100-150 bytes each) hangs 120 s then tracebacks instead of reporting the failure. Rare today, likelier with larger trees.
evidence: paramiko 3.x in the dashboard venv: common.py:232 DEFAULT_WINDOW_SIZE = 64*2**15; channel.py _check_add_window only from recv/recv_stderr; run_ssh call order.
fix: Drain both streams concurrently (recv_ready/recv_stderr_ready loop or a stderr reader thread), keeping the (rc, out, err) contract.

title: The 500 MB b-roll index is staged in /tmp on TrueNAS, the place the deploy moved its big artefacts away from
what: staging_parent returns /tmp on every non-DSM backend. OPS-8 says /tmp on the NAS may be RAM-backed and moved the 1.4 GB music artefacts to <apps root>/staging; broll.db is now 501 MB and is left in /tmp on every failure until a later deploy prunes it (>= 2 h old).
cost: 0.5 GB of /tmp per publish, 1-1.5 GB after a couple of failed retries until the next deploy; at ~20k clips (~2 GB index) a single publish can ENOSPC a small /tmp.
evidence: publish_db.py:608-609; install_dashboard_app.py:5244-5247, 5272-5276; measured index 501,460,992 bytes / 25,578 videos. /tmp's backing on the studio NAS not checked.
ledger: related to OPS-8 / SERVER-5 (fixed for the deploy only)
fix: Stage under <apps root>/staging on TrueNAS too; the existing prune glob already matches the publish slug.

title: bench/ no longer measures the lanes the companion ships, yet is installed and tested on every CI run
what: The harness sweeps --transfers, --multi-thread-streams and --sftp-chunk-size only; the shipped lanes also hinge on --sftp-concurrency (CR-364's DSM rule) and lane B's WebDAV remote_down route with a pinned --multi-thread-cutoff. bench imports nothing from the companion, so nothing flags the drift.
cost: A venv build from the lock plus 14 test files on every CI push (estimated 30-60 s runner time) for a tool that cannot reproduce CR-364 or evaluate the WebDAV route; misleading if used to pick a chunk size.
evidence: Flag builder vs companion rclone_lane.py:427-428, :643-645, :706-711; CI steps; last bench code change 2026-09-18.
fix: Add sftp_concurrency and a WebDAV endpoint kind to the matrix, or retire bench/ to legacy and drop its CI steps and run_all_tests row (keep check_health's peer_path copy, which is live).

title: The bootstrap re-fetches the site manifest the wizard already holds, and three keys come ONLY from that second fetch
what: Both bootstraps fetch /api/v1/site unconditionally even when launched by the wizard; rclone_remote, sftp_shell_type and sftp_hostkey have no flag and come only from that second fetch. install-onboard-2 closed this class for canonical_prefix/tree_name only.
cost: Per install: one extra round trip (up to 8 s). When the second fetch fails, config.toml gets the site's remote name (ensure_config, cached manifest) while rclone.conf gets [ccsync_sftp]: every lane A/B pass fails on a green install, and the stanza is written without known_hosts_file, so the lanes trust any NAS host key until a re-run.
evidence: Windows param block has no RcloneRemote/SftpShellType/SftpHostKey; run_bootstrap passes neither; the fetch at :872 is unconditional.
fix: Pass the wizard's manifest to the child (e.g. CCSYNC_SITE_JSON env) and have both scripts use it in place of their own fetch when present; hand-runs keep fetching.

title: Windows and macOS bootstraps implement the same steps twice and have drifted; move the drifted steps into the companion CLI
what: Drift: (1) companion currency check size+mtime on Windows vs sha256 on macOS; (2) macOS boots out the running companion before replacing it, Windows copies over the live exe; (3) Syncthing REST wait 20x(3 s timeout + 1 s) on Windows (message says 20 s) vs 10x1 s plus a fixed sleep 2 on macOS; (4) temp staging cleaned on macOS, not on Windows; (5) macOS loads the companion agent before repairing rclone_path while Windows seeds config before launch (lanes bake rclone_path at construction, so a fast-reading companion runs with a bare name launchd cannot resolve - plausible race); (6) Windows confirms the launched PID after 3 s, macOS does not; (7) pinned versions and sha256s duplicated with no parity test. Both config-seeding blocks are dead in the wizard flow (ensure_config writes first).
cost: Every installer fix lands twice (MAC-9, INST-7, GL-28, CR-372 precedents) and the list above is what slipped. Estimated ~750 lines out of the .ps1 and ~650 out of the .sh if manifest resolution, pinned download + verify (parallel in Python), rclone stanza, Syncthing seeding, config seed/repair and device-ID parse move to companion subcommands, as --setup-resolve-prefs already did.
evidence: Line references in the .md finding; each drift read in both files.
fix: Parity fixes first (sha256 on Windows, one bounded wait, launch after config repair on macOS, a pin parity test); then companion subcommands both scripts call, keeping the scripts runnable standalone.

title: macOS install waits for Resolve to quit twice, back to back, each up to 180 s
what: run_resolve_mapping and run_resolve_prefs each call wait_for_resolve_quit with the full 180 s budget; when the first times out, the second almost always times out too.
cost: Once per Mac install with Resolve open: 3 extra minutes of dead wait. Today pgrep -x "DaVinci Resolve" may never match (bug-resolve-5), so the waits may not run at all; fixing that turns this on.
evidence: Two call sites with no shared timed-out state.
fix: Remember the first wait's verdict and skip the second wait when it already timed out; fix together with bug-resolve-5.

title: The Windows pinned download leaves ~130 MB of zips and extracted folders in %TEMP%
what: The downloaded zip and the extract dir under %TEMP% are never removed and the uninstaller does not know them; macOS uses mktemp -d with a cleanup trap. A re-run re-downloads even when a verified zip is present.
cost: Once per fresh install: rclone ~23 MB zip + ~65 MB extracted, Syncthing ~13 MB + ~30 MB, about 130 MB (estimated) left behind.
evidence: No Remove-Item of $zipPath/$extractDir after the copy.
fix: try/finally removing both after the copy, or a per-run stage dir; optionally reuse a zip that passes Test-PinnedDownload.

title: A hand re-run of windows_bootstrap.ps1 with -CompanionExeSource aborts at step 9 while the companion is running
what: Copy-Item over the running companion exe, outside any try, under ErrorActionPreference=Stop: a terminating error when the bundled exe differs. Autostart, Resolve prefs, launch, device ID and the capability summary never run. The wizard path is unaffected (clean slate kills the companion first).
cost: Each documented hand re-run on a live editor machine ends in a red error with an exit code other than 3, read as a hard failure.
evidence: macOS twin boots the agent out first (:2520-2522); windows_upgrade.ps1 kills, renames aside and retries for this reason.
fix: Stop the running companion only when a copy is needed, rename the live exe aside, copy, and catch/warn on failure, as windows_upgrade.ps1 does.

title: windows_upgrade.ps1 runs a full recursive ACL reset inside the companion-down window every upgrade
what: Between the kill (:184) and the relaunch (:530) the script re-grants ~/.ccsync and runs icacls /reset /T over every file under it, plus two secret-file icacls and a fixed 800 ms sleep; the companion's own state_acl.repair_if_needed already probes at start and repairs only on a denial.
cost: Per manual upgrade per machine: grant 0.27 s + reset 0.55 s per 5,000 files (measured on a synthetic tree) + ~0.2 s + 0.8 s sleep added to tray downtime; grows with ~/.ccsync.
evidence: Probe in scratch: grant 266 ms, /reset /T over 5,000 files 555 ms; state_acl.py:12-17.
fix: Move the ACL repair and secret-file tightening after the relaunch-and-confirm, or gate the recursive reset on the denied-file probe; replace the 800 ms sleep with Wait-Process on the killed PIDs.

title: build_editor_package's onboard.exe staleness check ignores four bundled inputs
what: $onboardInputs covers onboarding/*.py, windows_bootstrap.ps1 and the companion exe only; the spec also bundles drive_mapping.ps1, windows_uninstall.ps1, EULA.md and the licence files, so a change to any of them reports onboard.exe up to date.
cost: On runs without -RebuildOnboard (ship.cmd and CI always rebuild): new editors get the old uninstaller / drive-ownership guard while the loose package files are new, under a green report.
evidence: Spec datas list vs $onboardInputs.
fix: Derive $onboardInputs from the spec's list, or glob installer\*.ps1 plus onboarding\assets and the licence files.

title: The base-rig wizard path never switches on Resolve's External scripting
what: CR-373's enable_resolve_scripting() (and --setup-resolve-prefs) run only in _worker_editor; the base finish page then always tells the user to set External scripting by hand.
cost: Every base-rig install: one manual Resolve preference, and a watcher/fixer/Cards agent that is silent until it is done.
evidence: The two worker bodies.
fix: Call steps.enable_resolve_scripting() in _worker_base after the companion install; it already refuses safely while Resolve runs.

title: Locked exe copies renamed to .stale-<epoch> by the clean slate are never pruned
what: Each wizard run that meets a locked companion exe leaves a ~48 MB .stale-<ts> copy; COMPANION_FILE_NAMES and every later cleanup omit the pattern, so each re-run can add another.
cost: Rare per run, unbounded over re-runs: ~48 MB each, under the bin dir, the local root or the tree drive root (the uninstaller removes only the bin dir).
evidence: Repo-wide grep for 'stale-': steps.py:3360 and one test only.
fix: Add a *.stale-* glob over the same candidate dirs to build_cleanup_plan's exe list.

title: ship.cmd runs the whole dashboard suite twice, the first time serially (~21.5 min per ship); in image mode the first run guards a deploy that does not happen
where: tools/ship.ps1:768-784 (step 0c, serial); tools/release.ps1:673-727 (step 2a, again with -n auto); tools/ship.ps1:831-848 (image mode decided after 0c)
what: GL-25 added a dashboard suite run before step 1, but release.ps1 still runs it again in step 2a, and step 0c has no -n auto --dist loadfile. On the image-mode studio step 1 deploys nothing, so 0c guards nothing.
cost: Every pathway-A ship (three companion versions cut on 2026-11-10) x ~19 min serial + ~2.5 min parallel = ~21.5 min of dashboard tests, ~19 min of it pure waste. select_suites.py rates today's two companion releases SCOPED (companion + 20 dashboard test files).
evidence: Both invocations read; CLAUDE.md 'Fast runs' (~19 min serial vs ~2.5 min parallel); select_suites.py --base 6b5c0c6 --head 5aee6ff -> SCOPED in 0.31 s.
fix: Run the dashboard suite once in 0c with -n auto --dist loadfile and pass release.ps1 a -SkipDashboardSuite; better, scope 0c with select_suites.py against the live code.commit (fail closed to FULL). Keep: a red suite stops the ship before any bind-mode deploy.

title: With the linux CI job off, 'ci.yml green on the exact commit' no longer covers the dashboard/server/tools/web suites or the CRLF, licence and notices gates, yet release_customers.py publishes a dashboard bundle to every customer on it
what: A job skipped by if: false leaves the run 'success', and every release gate reads only the run conclusion.
